articles.title: Rahul Gandhi's 'PM Se Nipat Lenge' Remarks Spark Debate
articles.description: Rahul Gandhi's recent remarks, including his statement "PM Se Nipat Lenge," have sparked a political debate in India. The comments were made during a gathering at his residence, where he urged opposition leaders and activists to prepare for mobilization within 24 hours. This call for action was reportedly part of the India Bloc's strategy to protest against alleged electoral irregularities. However, Gandhi's subsequent departure to Vietnam has drawn criticism from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which claims his actions reflect a foreign-inspired strategy. Rahul Gandhi's 'PM Se Nipat Lenge' Remarks During the meeting, Gandhi emphasized the need for sustained protests and youth mobilization, urging participants to be ready for flash demonstrations and confrontations. His remarks, including the phrase "PM Se Nipat Lenge," were interpreted by the BJP as a direct challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah. The BJP has alleged that Gandhi's approach mirrors unrest seen in countries like France and Bangladesh, suggesting a playbook for political agitation. Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chauhan questioned Gandhi's credentials, while Congress leaders like Shashi Tharoor refuted claims of advocating violent regime change. Congress Denies Allegations of Anarchy Congress leaders have dismissed the BJP's accusations, asserting that their aim is to ensure free and fair elections rather than instigate chaos. Tharoor stated that India is neither France nor Bangladesh, emphasizing the opposition's commitment to peaceful democratic processes. Meanwhile, Congress veteran Anand Sharma underscored the importance of constitutional frameworks for government change, rejecting any notion of regime change outside electoral processes. Gandhi's reported Vietnam trip has further fueled criticism, with questions raised about his commitment to the movement he initiated. The debate continues as political tensions rise ahead of upcoming elections.

articles.title: 'No Loyalty To Pak?': Khawaja Asif Sounds Alarm Over Bureaucrats' Exodus To US, Canada, Europe
articles.description: Pakistan may be sinking, and the first to sense it may be its own elite. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has raised the alarm over what he calls a bureaucratic exodus, accusing senior officers of arranging to settle in Canada, the United States, Britain and Europe while still serving the state. He singled out Portugal, claiming influential officials have prepared their families and finances for relocation, and asked whether they are truly loyal to Pakistan or merely in transit. It is not his first charge: in August 2025, he alleged that over half of the senior bureaucracy had bought property or sought citizenship there. Meanwhile, GDP growth is 3.65 percent, external debt is 137.55 billion dollars and reserves cover two months of imports. The government has published no verified list of those allegedly leaving. articles.title: 'Paris Will Turn Muslim Soon': Trump Blames Immigration For France Riots; Macron Blames Iran War
articles.description: Paris is on fire, and Donald Trump has turned France's unrest into an immigration battle. Trump tells Emmanuel Macron he should have closed his borders, claiming Paris will be a Muslim city very soon. Macron has a very different explanation: rising fuel prices, a cost-of-living crisis and the fallout of the war in Iran. Around 200,000 people joined protests, including nearly 40,000 in Paris, and about 2,400 were arrested over the weekend. Cars burned, shops were looted and a historic city hall was engulfed in flames. French authorities blame far-left radicals and criminal groups, while student groups and Yellow Vest activists plan more protests under the slogan Macron must go. So is France burning because of migration, or because people can no longer afford to live? Here is everything you need to know. Watch the story and tell us what you think in the comments.
